messages.subject: Matrix occupancy model - missing visits/values
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Thanks for the help! I've got an occupancy model with p and Psi covariates that I set up using matrices rather than vectors for convenience.

Most sites have 3 visits per year in each of three years, so I have a response variable array of:
y[1:n_sites , 1:n_species , 1:2 (years), 1:3 (surveys per year)]

However, some sites (e.g. 5%) were only surveyed twice in a given year, and a few (3%) were only surveyed in one or two (rather than all three) years. I think all of the NAs in those years are giving me problems though I can't pinpoint exactly where/why. For example, I'm not getting estimates of my covariate coefficients (they are stuck at initial values).

So my main question is how I should be dealing with those missing values. One solution I tried (in for the formula below) is to index year and survey numbers for each site. For years I do this with a years-per-site vector (yrs), and for surveys per year I do this with a matrix of k[1:n_sites,1:n years] that shows how many visits there were.

This should prevent the model from ever encountering the missing data, but then the parameter matrices that it is estimating are not 'full', and I assume that is causing the model to fail (as it does when using the code below).

Note: this model also involves some latent variables, which you can ignore

#Psi model
for (yr in 1:(yrs[j])) {
  eta[j,i,yr] <-  inprod(u.b[i,1:Vocc], Xocc[j, ,yr]) + inprod(lv.coef[i,1:nlv],LV[j,1:nlv])
  u[j,i,yr] ~ dnorm(eta[j,i,yr],1/(1-sum(lv.coef[i,1:nlv]^2)))
  z[j,i,yr] <- step(u[j,i,yr])
}

#p model
for (yr in 1:(yrs[j])) {
  for (kv in 1:(k[j,yr])) {
    logit(p[j,i,yr,kv]) <-   inprod(v.b[i,1:Vobs], Xobs[j, ,yr,kv])
    mu.p[j,i,yr,kv] <- p[j,i,yr,kv]*z[j,i,yr]
    y[j,i,yr,kv] ~ dbern(mu.p[j,i,yr,kv])
  }
}

Is there a better way to deal with these missing surveys and years at some sites? Or am I stuck using a vector setup of this model?

The answer to the above question may also answer my other question, but I occasionally have missing p and Psi covariates as well. I don't care about estimates for these values except to the extent that Nimble needs them to get estimates for the parameters of interest for those sites. If I need to specify priors for those values can I ask the model to estimate mean and sd of each covariate column to create a prior? And do I need to give a formula in the model that is 'solved' for those missing values (which would be annoying for models with many covariates and a few missing values in each)? Or can Nimble use the information it already has (equations containing those covariates) to infer their values?

Thank you!

> Dear Quresh,

> Thanks for posting the question.
>
> It's hard to say without seeing more about your initial values.  In general, nimble is sensitive to the need for valid initial values, and there are cases where JAGS can recover but nimble can't recover.  Here is an example of how your initial values could potentially cause a problem.  If Z[j,i] is 0, then z[j, i] == n.point[j] is impossible and will have log probability of -Inf.  Sometimes an MCMC can recover from invalid initial values, sometimes not.  If psi[j, i] comes from an inverse logit, there can be numerical underflow that makes psi[j,i] exactly zero instead of just very very small, and that could also cause such a problem.
>
> You can use the nimble model in R to investigate where you have a problem (but you will have to use nimbleModel explicitly, not simply nimbleMCMC).  If model is the object returned from nimbleModel, you can explore it like:
> model$calculate() # check if the entire model is valid
> model$calculate("z")
> model$calculate( model$expandNodeNames("z[1, ]") )
> model$calculate("z[1, 1]") # These are examples of calculating the sum of log probabilities for parts of a model to see where there might be a problem.
> model$z # inspect model variables, especially values such as psi[j, i] and Z[j, i] to see if anything is being set to 0
>
> The user manual has more about how you can use models.
>
> I hope that helps.  If you investigate further and you're still stuck, please provide a reproducible example either on-list or off-list.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ryan,

For the first problem, can you report more about how the model fails?  Is there an error message in R or does it fail in the C++ compilation step?  The idea of using a vector of start and/or end indices to manage a ragged array is a typical and good way to handle what you need, but it's hard to tell without more information what is going wrong.  A minimal reproducible example would be the most helpful.  One possible thing that caught my eye is the empty index in Xobs.  Sometimes nimble can handle that, depending on what you've provided, and sometimes you would need to insert something like "1:N" explicitly.

For the second issue, I think this is more of a statistical question.  Sometimes with missing covariates, one makes a part of the model for the distribution of the covariates, in which the covariates are the "response", i.e. they are on the left-hand side of a stochastic declaration.  Then a missing covariate, entered into nimble as data with value NA, will be sampled by the MCMC, effectively integrating over its distribution as informed by other values of the covariate.  I hope that helps.

Perry

Hello all,

I am trying to run a relatively simple beta-binomial regression using nimble but I keep running into the same error so something must be eluding me although I’ve checked my calculations multiple times. I have tried both parametrizations of the beta distribution supported by nimble (i.e. with shape1 & shape2 and also with mu and sd, as it is specified in the user manual), but to no avail.

Here is the likelihood statement for each of the parametrizations

#Likelihood mu-sd parametrization

for (i in 1:n.obs){

#Number of success from binomial distribution with prob[i] as prob and trials as number of trials

y[i] ~ dbinom(prob=prob[i], size=trials[i])

#Prob prob[i] follows beta distribution with mean mu[i] and sd = sig (The manual states that Nimble supports this parametrization for the beta distribution)

prob[i] ~ dbeta(mean=mu[i],sd=sig)

#Logit mean probability is predicted by year and ID-level random effect

logit(mu[i]) <- yr2020 + beta2019 * yr2019[i] + beta2021 * yr2021[i] + epsID[ID[i]]

}

#Likelihood shape1 shape2 parametrization

for (i in 1:n.obs){

y[i]~ dbinom(prob=prob[i], size=trials[i])

logit(mu[i]) <- yr2020 + beta2019 * yr2019[i] + beta2021 * yr2021[i] + epsID[ID[i]]

prob[i] ~ dbeta(shape1=a[i],shape2=b[i])

    a[i] <- mu[i]^2 * (1-mu[i]) / sig^2 - mu[i]

    b[i] <- mu[i] * (1 - mu[i])^2 / sig^2 + mu[i] - 1

  }

I keep getting an error saying that there is a NaN in the proportion generated by the beta distribution. There are 2 errors, I get

Checking model calculations

NaNs were detected in model variable: logProb_prob.

Then, when the MCMC runs, all prob[i] nodes are not initialized well and result in a NA or NaN. I feel like there is a problem in the values I feed to the beta distribution but I’m not so sure where to look next. I managed to run the exact same model in JAGS (except I have non-centered random effects for the individual level, but this should’nt make a difference, right?) and everything works just fine. However the parametrization for dbeta() is a bit different in jags so that might be where I’m having a problem with Nimble. I know I could just use the JAGS model for my paper but I’m very curious as to why I’m not able to write it properly in Nimble (and I’d rather cite Nimble ;) ).

Thanks for any help with this, I have attached my code and a sample of my dataset so that anyone can reproduce the errors.

Cheers,

Fred L.

Consider the following transition probability matrix (TPM) for individuals i and surveys t:

# Alive in state 1
TPM[1,1,i,t] <- phi1[i,t] * (1 - psi12[i,t])  # Survives, remains in state 1
TPM[1,2,i,t] <- phi1[i,t] * psi12[i,t]          # Survives, transition to state 2
TPM[1,3,i,t] <- 1 - phi1[i,t]                       # Dies in state 1

# Alive in state 2
TPM[2,1,i,t] <- phi2[i,t] * psi21[i,t]          # Survives, transitions to state 1
TPM[2,2,i,t] <- phi2[i,t] * (1 - psi21[i,t])  # Survives, remains in state 2
TPM[2,3,i,t] <- 1 - phi2[i,t]                       # Dies in state 2

# Dead (state 3)
TPM[3,1,i,t] <- 0                                       # Transitions to state 1
TPM[3,2,i,t] <- 0                                       # Transition to state 2
TPM[3,3,i,t] <- 1                                       # Dies

Here, phi1 and phi2 are the survival probabilities of individuals in state 1 and 2, respectively, and psi12 and psi21 are the state transition probabilities between state 1 and state 2 and between state 2 and state 1, respectively. Sometimes, it is better to formulate TPMs as transition rate matrices (TRMs), where state transitions are formulated as hazard rates (Miller & Anderson 2008 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2008.00996.x>, Conn et al 2012 <http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10336-010-0591-z>, Ergon et al. 2018 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13059>). The TRM corresponding to the THM above is the following:

# Alive in state 1
TRM[1,1,i,t] <- -(psi12[i,t] + phi1[i,t])  # Survives, remains in state 1
TRM[1,2,i,t] <- psi12[i,t]                       # Survives, transition to state 2
TRM[1,3,i,t] <- phi1[i,t]                         # Dies in state 1

# Alive in state 2
TRM[2,1,i,t] <- psi21[i,t]                       # Survives, transitions to state 1
TRM[2,2,i,t] <- -(psi21 + phi2[i,t])       # Survives, remains in state 2
TRM[2,3,i,t] <- phi2[i,t]                         # Dies in state 2

# Dead (state 3)
TRM[3,1,i,t] <- 0                                     # Transitions to state 1
TRM[3,2,i,t] <- 0                                     # Transition to state 2
TRM[3,3,i,t] <- 0                                     # Dies

Here, phi1 and phi2 are the mortality hazard rates and psi12 and psi21 are the hazard rates of transitioning between the two states.

You can convert a TRM to a TPM with the matrix exponential function, where TPM = exp(TRM * Delta), where Delta is the time interval between successive surveys. One of the benefits of using the hazard rate formulation is that apparently, it fully accounts for unequal time intervals. I don't understand how this works, however. Nimble does not have a built-in matrix exponential function, and although one can use expm::expm() using nimbleRcall, this approach is approximately 10x slower than using nimble's built-in matrix functions (in my very brief testing).

exp(TRM * Delta) can be rewritten as V %*% exp(D * Delta) %*% V^-1, where V is the matrix of eigenvectors of the TRM and D is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues of D. Note that we're still dealing with a matrix exponential function of D * Delta, but this is easy to manually specify in nimble by simply taking the exponential function of each diagonal element. So in nimbleCode, we do the following:

# Matrix of eigenvectors of TRM
V[1:3,1:3,i,t] <- eigen(TRM[1:3,1:3,i,t])$vectors

# Diagonal matrix of eigenvalues of TRM
D[1:3,1:3,i,t] <- diag(eigen(TRM[1:3,1:3,i,t])$values)

# Exponential of D * Delta
expD[1,1,i,t] <- exp(D[1,1,i,t] * Delta[t])
expD[1,2,i,t] <- 0
expD[1,3,i,t] <- 0
expD[2,1,i,t] <- 0
expD[2,2,i,t] <- exp(D[2,2,i,t] * Delta[t])
expD[2,3,i,t] <- 0
expD[3,1,i,t] <- 0
expD[3,2,i,t] <- 0
expD[3,3,i,t] <- exp(D[3,3,i,t] * Delta[t])

# Create TPM from TRM
TPM[1:3,1:3,i,t] <- V[1:3,1:3,i,t] %*% expD[1:3,1:3,i,t] %*% inverse(V[1:3,1:3,i,t])

Now, we can use the TPM in likelihood as usual, e.g., z[i,t] ~ dcat(TPM[1:3,1:3,i,t-1]).

Hopefully this method is indeed correct! Even with the built-in matrix functions, this model runs way slower than just specifying the TPM with probabilities. A model that took 1 day to run previously is looking like it will run for 8 days now.

Kind regards,

Matt

messages.subject: Re: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Yes, there are several different points when you can change the frequency of the adaptation interval for adaptive samplers.  Most simply, this will affect all samplers in an MCMC, (see section 7.2.2.3 "Overriding the default sampler control list values" of the user manual), when you first call configureMCMC, provide the "control" argument, and specify the new adaptation interval, as:

mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, control = list(adaptInterval = 100))

This will make all adaptive MCMC samplers in that MCMC configuration use an adaptation interval of every-100-iterations, instead of the default value of every-200-iterations.  Advantage: adaptation will take place twice as often, and samplers may (in theory) approach their optimal mixing performance faster.  Disadvantages: more computation required for the adaptation procedures (as you mentioned; although this is essentially negligible for all univariate samplers, and only plays a real factor for multivariate samplers, for example the RW_block sampler), and also that each adaptation phase will be using *half as much information* on which to base its adaptation of internal parameters.  In contrast, the default of every-200-iterations will (in theory) make "more educated" adaptations, albeit half as often, because it's using the information from the most recent 200 iterations for its calculations.  But it's an open question in what situations larger or smaller adaptation intervals are preferable, and certainly is case dependent.

You can also change the adaptation interval of individual samplers, by adding them to the MCMC configuration, as:

conf$addSampler(type = SAMPLERTYPE, target = NODE, adaptInterval = 100)

Good questions, keep at it,
Daniel

Thanks,
Alison

#declaring a nimbleList object with types
hom_list <- nimbleList(mu_bar = double(2),
lam_bar = double(2),
mu_data = double(2))

assign('hom_list', hom_list, envir = .GlobalEnv)

#homogenization

Z,
alpha_mu,
W,
gamma_lambda,
usfact,
cell_numbers
){
fs_cells <- raster::raster(matrix(Z[,2:ncol(Z)],nrow=100,ncol=100))
mu <- exp(Z%*%alpha_mu)
lambda <- W%*%gamma_lambda/mu
fs_cells$mu <- mu
fs_cells$lambda <- lambda
mu_bar <- raster::aggregate(fs_cells$mu,
fact = as.integer(usfact),
fun = function(x,na.rm){(1/mean(1/x,na.rm=TRUE))})
lambda_bar <- mu_bar*raster::aggregate(fs_cells$lambda,
fact = as.integer(usfact),
fun = function(x,na.rm){(mean(x,na.rm=TRUE))})
# This gives the values at the coordinates of the data
mu_data <- mu[cell_numbers]

hom_list$mu_bar <- raster::as.matrix(mu_bar)
hom_list$lambda_bar <- raster::as.matrix(lambda_bar)
hom_list$mu_data <- raster::as.matrix(mu_data)

return(hom_list)
}

W = double(2),

usfact= double(0),
cell_numbers = double(1)
){},

returnType = hom_list
)

Totally reasonable.  If the adaptationInterval (another variable internal to the sampler, which doesn't change) is at its default value of 200, then every 200 MCMC iterations, the adaptation procedure will take place (internal to the sampler).  This includes updating the scale (proposal standard deviation) parameter based on the past 200 posterior samples, and also setting timesRan (which means times ran since the most recent adaptation took place - not the total times ran) and timesAccepted (similar interpretation) back to 0.  We can see timesAdapted is exactly what we'd expect: adaptationInterval * timesAdapted = 200 * 75 = 15,000 total MCMC iterations.  If you ran it for 15,001 iterations, you would see timesRan = 1, and timesAccepted would be either 0 or 1.  So everything is bang on looks like it's working fine.

messages.subject: Spatiotemporal hierarchical BYM model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm currently trying to build a BYM spatiotemporal model with Type II and III interaction terms and struggling to adapt my code for a Type I interaction. I wondered if anyone would be willing to share any template code for Type II and III interactions?

Thank you!

This is my code that runs well for the Type I interaction:

#write the spatiotemporal model
st_typeI_BYMmodel <- nimbleCode(
  {
    for (i in 1:N)
    {
      for(t in 1:Temporal)
      {

        O[i,t]  ~ dpois(mu[i,t])
        log(mu[i,t]) <- log(E[i,t]) + alpha + theta[i] + phi[i] + gamma[t] + xi[t] + zeta[i, t]

        zeta[i, t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.zeta)
        gamma[t] ~ dnorm(0,tau.gamma)

        residRRtm[t] <- exp(gamma[t] + xi[t])
        residRRtypeI[i, t] <- exp(zeta[i, t])

        RR[i,t] <- exp(alpha + theta[i] + phi[i] + gamma[t] + xi[t] + zeta[i, t])

      }

      theta[i] ~ dnorm(0,tau.theta)
      residRR[i] <- exp(theta[i] + phi[i])
      PP[i] <- step(residRR[i]-1)
    }

    # intrinsic CAR prior on temporal random effects
    xi[1:Temporal] ~ dcar_normal(adj.tm <http://adj.tm>[1:K], weights.tm <http://weights.tm>[1:K], num.tm <http://num.tm>[1:Temporal], tau.xi, zero_mean = 1)

    # intrinsic CAR prior on spatial random effects
    phi[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tau.phi, zero_mean = 1)

    # priors
    alpha  ~ dflat()
    overallRR <- exp(alpha)

    # temporal field
    tau.gamma~ dgamma(1,0.001)
    sigma2.gamma <- 1/tau.gamma

    tau.xi ~ dgamma(0.5,0.005)
    sigma2.xi <- 1/tau.xi

    # spatial field
    tau.theta ~ dgamma(1,0.001)
    sigma2.theta <- 1/tau.theta

    tau.phi ~ dgamma(0.5,0.005)
    sigma2.phi <- 1/tau.phi

    # spatiotemporal field
    tau.zeta ~ dgamma(1,0.001)
    sigma2.zeta <- 1/tau.zeta
  }
)

#specify initial values (adding in zeta term)
inits <- list(
  list(alpha = 1,
       tau.theta = 10,
       tau.phi = 1,
       tau.xi = 8,
       tau.gamma = 5,
       tau.zeta = 5,
       theta = rep(0.02, times = N),
       phi = c(rep(0.2, times = N)),
       gamma = rep(0.02, times = Temporal),
       xi = c(rep(0.2, times = Temporal)),
       zeta = matrix(0.2, nrow = N, ncol = Temporal)
  ),
  list(alpha = 0.5,
       tau.theta = 1,
       tau.phi = 0.1,
       tau.xi = 0.8,
       tau.gamma = 0.5,
       tau.zeta = 1,
       theta = rep(0.05, times = N),
       phi = c(rep(-0.05, times = N)),
       gamma = rep(-0.02, times = Temporal),
       xi = c(rep(-0.2, times = Temporal)),
       zeta = matrix(-0.2, nrow = N, ncol = Temporal)
  )
)

#add zeta to parameters to monitor
params <- c("overallRR", "RR","residRR", "PP", "sigma2.phi",
            "sigma2.theta", "phi", "theta", "xi", "gamma",
            "sigma2.gamma", "sigma2.xi", "mu", "residRRtm",
            "residRRtypeI", "sigma2.zeta", "zeta")

#run the MCMC
t_0 <- Sys.time()
st_typeI_BYM.model <- nimbleMCMC(code = st_typeI_BYMmodel,
                                 data = GSdata,
                                 constants = GSConsts,
                                 inits = inits,
                                 monitors = params,
                                 niter = ni,
                                 nburnin = nb,
                                 thin = nt,
                                 nchains = nc,
                                 setSeed = 9,
                                 progressBar = TRUE,
                                 samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,
                                 summary = TRUE,
                                 WAIC = TRUE
)
t_1 <- Sys.time()
t_1 - t_0

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for the clear explanation.  First thing is please try updating nimble if you haven't done so recently.  There was a bug fix for 0.12-2 that might fix this case.

If that doesn't work, I'd suggest doing it like this:

y.event <- nimArray(dim = c(M.both, J, 3), init=FALSE)
for(i in 1:3) {
 y.event[1:M.both, 1:J, i] <- model$y.event[t,1:M.both,1:J, i] # "chipping" or subsetting down to 2D from the original 3D should allow the assignment to work.
}

Then do your work with y.event and use a similar for-loop to put values back into the model if needed.

Alternatively you can work with values directly out of the model in 2D subsets (i.e. not even making a copy) if needed.

Here is what I think is confusing about the messages.  nimble can do element-wise math with anything up to 2D, including 2D chips of higher-dimensional objects.  Assignment is included in "doing math".  So the y.full line of your first message worked because you have a 2D subset of a 3D object, so it could do the assignment.  Now, actually *assignment* for higher dimensional objects is the one kind of operation that is, or was supposed to be, supported.  However there was a recent bug where in some situations it wouldn't work, and that was fixed.  I think that fix will cover your case, but from only looking at it briefly I am not sure and could be wrong (please let me know!).  So a solution is to access the higher dimension object using indexing to get down to 2 or fewer dimensions at a time, including for copying.  I hope that helps.

-Perry

Hi Ryan,

I don't have time at the moment to dig into the details of your code/what you are doing, but a few brief comments:

1) It is very likely a problem if you are getting messages about -Inf as logProb values during the MCMC. Often this would indicate that there are invalid parameter values.

2) While missing initial values (i.e., NAs) may not be a problem in some cases, in that Nimble can draw from the prior to fill them in, it's usually a good idea to initialize everything to reasonable values. So that may be a good place to start.

3) As far as padding your arrays, presumably your model doesn't actually use the padded elements, so either 0 or NA may be fine. But it may be safest to put in zeros.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alison,

Sorry for the delay getting into this.  It looks like our documentation makes it look like all types are supported, but really only numeric types are successfully translated from C++ to R and/or R to C++ in a nimbleRcall.  Here is a workaround you could use to store multiple results in R and then use getter functions to pull each one into C++ (i.e. in a compiled nimbleFunction).  Within the nimbleFunction they could be put into a nimbleList if it is still useful (but you might have only wanted that for the returnType purpose in the first place).

-Perry

--------------------------
library(nimble)

make_my_funs <- function() {
  # Using R's lexical scoping, the three functions
  # returned by this function share ans1 and ans2
  # in their enclosing environment.  You could alternatively
  # use the R Global environment.
  ans1 <- matrix(0.1, nrow = 0, ncol = 0) # The 0.1 makes it numeric
  ans2 <- numeric()
  # do_stuff will do the interesting work and store the results
  # to be returned by separate functions.
  do_stuff <- function(x) {
    ans1 <<- x %o% x # Make a matrix result.  Note non-local assignment.
    ans2 <<- sum(x)  # Make a scalar result.  Ditto.
  }
  get_ans1 <- function() ans1
  get_ans2 <- function() ans2
  list(do_stuff = do_stuff,
       get_ans1 = get_ans1,
       get_ans2 = get_ans2)
}

my_funs <- make_my_funs()
do_stuff <- my_funs$do_stuff
get_ans1 <- my_funs$get_ans1
get_ans2 <- my_funs$get_ans2
nim_do_stuff <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(1)) {}, Rfun = "do_stuff", returnType = void())
nim_get_ans1 <- nimbleRcall(function() {}, Rfun = "get_ans1", returnType = double(2))
nim_get_ans2 <- nimbleRcall(function() {}, Rfun = "get_ans2", returnType = double(0))

# Make a nimbleFunction to use the three nimbleRcalls.
# (This shows how you would use them in a sampler. In a custom function or
# distribution, remove the setup line.)
nf_test <- nimbleFunction(
  setup = function() {},
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    nim_do_stuff(x)
    ans1 <- nim_get_ans1()
    ans2 <- nim_get_ans2()
    # could put these into a nimbleList if helpful.
    cat("ans2 = ", ans2, "\n")
    return(ans1)
    returnType(double(2))
  }
)

nf_test1 <- nf_test()
Cnf_test1 <- compileNimble(nf_test1)

x <- as.numeric(1:3)
Cnf_test1$run(1:3)

# Test this as a non-setup function
nf_test2 <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    nim_do_stuff(x)
    ans1 <- nim_get_ans1()
    ans2 <- nim_get_ans2()
    # could put these into a nimbleList if helpful.
    cat("ans2 = ", ans2, "\n")
    return(ans1)
    returnType(double(2))
  }
)

Cnf_test2 <- compileNimble(nf_test2)
Cnf_test2(x)

Hi Brook,

I'll add to this.  I have seen other cases where people want to do something like you are suggesting.  Often the solution is to say that if x[i] follows a distribution and your observed data is f(x[i]), then you need to use distribution theory to derive what is the distribution of f(x[i]) and write a distribution function to calculate that. If you are completely sure you want it to look like what you wrote, you could do a trick like the following:

  x[i] <- f(i,data[1:n])

   dummy[i] ~ ddistribution(x[i], parameters)

where dummy[i] is some value playing the role of data in the graphical model but whose value you don't even use.  When you write a custom distribution called "ddistribution", it will be called as:

ddisttribution(dummy[i], x[i], parameters, log = TRUE)

and the value it returns will contribute to the log probability of the graphical model.  The "dummy[i]" is in the first argument so it is syntactically where the datum value usually goes.  But you are free to write ddistribution to ignore it and use the first "parameter", x[i], as the datum in whatever calculation you want.  Be sure to provide the dummy variable as data when you create the model.

Again, this is often not really what one wants, but I'm just telling you how you can arrange it if you are sure it is what you want.

HTH.
-Perry

Thanks Chris for jumping in here.  Ryan, my apologies that your thread went hanging unanswered.  We try hard to respond to everyone but recently we've been very busy and this slipped past me.

I will just add a bit to what Chris said.  Usually the warning messages come from some kind of incomplete or invalid inits.  Nimble generally benefits from complete inits.  Sometimes an MCMC can recover and start exploring sets of valid values and then operate correctly.  Often it can't.  The way to check is to see how the mixing looks, but that includes mixing of latent states that you might not be monitoring by default.  Usually if it is stuck in invalid values, then some nodes will not mix at all.  A good strategy to be sure your results are valid and also to gain confidence that your model is in order is to track down why there are incomplete or invalid inits. You can use the model object in R to do so.  If you want to browse through previous postings on nimble-users, you might find other examples of doing this.  Often it looks something like the following.

# Assume model was returned from nimbleModel.
model$calculate() #Somewhere you get warnings or -Infs, or you get these when you call nimbleMode with default calculate = TRUE.
# If you get a message saying there is an issue with a node z[1, 2, 3], check it:
model$z[1, 2, 3]
model$calculate("z[1, 2, 3]")
# Then check its parent nodes.  Maybe it depends on a node called prob[1, 2, 3], so check and re-calculate that
model$prob[1, 2, 3]
# etc. and the idea is by studying each node and sequence of calculations from one node to another, you
# can determine where some init is missing or has a value that is resulting in a NA or -Inf in a later calculation.

# If you do not get a clear message on where there is a problem node, you can track it down by calculating narrower and narrower parts of the model.
model$calculate("z") # will do all z nodes and reveal if there is a problem somewhere
model$calculate("z[1, , ]") will do this subset of z nodes, etc.
# You can also look at the log probabilities of stochastic nodes to help see where there was a problem
model$logProb_z

I hope that helps.  Thanks for providing your code.  Would it work for you to try this strategy and then get back to us if you are still stuck and one of us can dive into your code at that point?

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hey Iraida,

Let me try to answer your question with a recent application I had. I did a multisite capture-recapture model with just three sites. I wanted to partial pool the parameters across sites, so I specified random site effects for survival, state transitions, and recapture. I did this because I didn't want the model to estimate all parameters separately for each site without the model 'knowing' what's happening for these parameters at the other sites. So for phi, I specified:

for(m in 1:n.site){
   phi.eps[m] ~ dnorm(0, sd = phi.sigma)
   logit(phi[m]) <- phi.alpha + phi.eps[m]
}

However, knowing that I had only three sites, I wasn't actually interested in the hyperparameters (phi.alpha and phi.sigma), because a huge range of values in each parameter could explain my observations of only three sites. For this reason as well, the parameters phi.alpha and phi.sigma don't mix well and don't really converge. However, when I monitor phi[m], the site-specific parameters, I get perfect convergence. So the model is able to converge on your site-level parameters but not the hyperparameters governing them. In my case this is fine; I wanted to partial pool to get "better" estimates for the site-specific parameters, but I wasn't interested in inferring larger trends from the hyperparameters.

I haven't seen much written about this stuff, and I'd love to know if other people have thoughts as well. However, from my experience, it's OK if some parameters don't converge. Just don't make inferences on these parameters, and make sure the parameters you're actually interested in (in my case, the site-specific parameters) do converge.

Hope this helps a little.

Cheers,

Matt

I wanted to partial pool the parameters across sites, so I specified random site effects for survival, state transitions, and recapture. I did this because I didn't want the model to estimate all parameters separately for each site without the model 'knowing' what's happening for these parameters at the other sites. Hi Chris,

JAGS sometimes does a better job of initializing parameter values than does nimble when the user doesn't provide initial values for all stochastic quantities in the model and there are vague priors.

I took a quick look at your code, and I see that there are various quantities that you are not explicitly initializing, such as 'qe'. Please try providing initial values for everything (or at least for everything with a vague prior) and see if that fixes things. You'll want to be able to run CSGCM$calculate() and get a numerical value back before starting the MCMC.

-chris

Hi Keith, I think the following is probably the best path forward.

Instead of assigning dnorm to the transformed observations, create a user-defined distribution that calculates the density of the original observations. This is akin to using a lognormal distribution on a set of observations rather than a normal distribution on log-transformed observations.  The Jacobian  based on your transformation will be calculated in the user-defined distribution and combined with the dnorm density (which is akin to how one would derive the lognormal distribution as well).

Then the WAIC comparison should just work, since you can just get it from nimble under the beta model and under this other model.

-chris

Hi Gates,

Another thing that can take a while is the configuration stage--the argument useConjugacy=FALSE while passing something to configureMCMC can also speed up model building a lot.

Sampling the "unsampled" N's adds unnecessary calculations, but unless there are a lot of these, I doubt it's a substantial issue. Could use dynamic indexing to cut out some of these (i.e., only loop over the specific years sampled or the number of years sampled for a given site) if you wanted. Would reorder the looping for N to do this (e.g., site, nyears[site], species).

Cheers,

John
